Nevertheless, the indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were significant and in the predicted direction for both positive and negative reputational perception. This pattern suggests that, particularly for negative reputational perception, other factors operating in the opposite direction may offset the country difference attributable to relational mobility.

One limitation of Studies 1a and 1b is that they assessed only participants' perceptions of how prevalent the sharing of reputational information was in their local social environments. Such perceptions may be biased and may not accurately reflect others' actual sharing behaviour in everyday life. It therefore remains unclear whether the predicted associations also extend to people's own sharing behaviour. To address this issue, in Study 2 we examined not only perceived prevalence as in Studies 1a and 1b, but also participants' self-reported everyday sharing of positive and negative reputational information as a complementary measure.

Study 2 Method

Participants and Design

We conducted a cross-societal questionnaire survey in Japan and the US in September 2023.

Two hundred participants per country were recruited via online platforms (Japan: Lancers; US: Connect by CloudResearch). Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation.

Because this survey was also embedded in a questionnaire designed for other projects conducted by our research team, the sample size was determined by those projects rather than by an a priori power analysis. Following Lakens (2022), we therefore conducted sensitivity power analyses as in Studies 1a and 1b to determine the smallest effect sizes detectable with the final samples at a specified level of power. With α = .05 and power of .80, the minimum detectable between-country difference was

Cohen's d = 0.29 for the final sample (N = 374), based on a two-tailed independent-samples t-test. For the mediation analyses, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations based on a single-mediator model with country (standardised) as the predictor and perceived relational mobility as the mediator, assuming no direct effect (c' = 0) and no covariates, as ARS was not controlled in Study 2. Because these assumptions were common to all four outcomes (the perceived prevalence and self-reported sharing of positive and negative reputational information), the results apply equally to each outcome. When the standardised a path ranged from .20 to .50, the sample had 80% power to detect a standardised b path of approximately .15-.17, corresponding to standardised indirect effects (ab) of .03-.08, using Monte Carlo confidence intervals. A check using bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals yielded power of .82 at a = .30 and b = .152 (ab = .046) (see Supplementary Materials, Table S1).

Prior to analysis, we excluded participants based on the same criteria used in Studies 1a and 1b, except that careless responding was assessed using only the first item (i.e., 'We want to test your attention, so please click on the answer 'Disagree''). We excluded 0 participants for criterion (a), 2 for (b), 0 for (c), 6 for (d), 15 for (e), and 2 for (f). We additionally excluded one participant with a missing variable. The final analytic sample consisted of 374 participants (Japan: N = 178, 86 men, 92 women; Mage = 43.11, SD = 10.27; US: N = 196, 110 men, 81 women, 5 others; Mage = 38.09, SD = 12.53).

Measures

We used three scales. The Relational Mobility Scale (Yuki et al., 2007) and the Positive and Negative Reputational Perception Scale (Kusakabe et al., 2024) were identical to those used in Studies 1a and 1b. These scales were scored in the same way as in Studies 1a and 1b. Additionally, we developed the Positive and Negative Reputational Communication Scale to assess participants' self-reported sharing of positive and negative reputational information. Specifically, we adapted the Positive and Negative Reputational Perception Scale by replacing third-person references (i.e. 'they') with firstperson references (i.e. 'I'). Example items included: 'I often talk about the strengths, achievements, and contributions of other people when those people are not around' and 'I actively say negative things about and criticize people who behave selfishly towards others, such as taking credit for things they did not do or refusing to help others when they are in need'. The scale consisted of five positive and five negative items. We averaged the five items for each subscale separately, with higher scores indicating a greater self-reported tendency to share positive or negative reputational information, respectively.

Japanese participants completed the survey in Japanese, and US participants completed it in English.

Responses to all three scales were recorded on a six-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree,6 = strongly agree). Participants also reported their demographic information.

Results

In the pooled Study 2 sample, all scales showed high internal consistency (relational mobility: α = .89, positive reputational perception: α = .91, negative reputational perception: α = .89, positive reputational communication: α = .93, negative reputational communication: α = .85). Participants' selfreported sharing was positively associated with their perceptions of others' sharing of information of the same valence in both countries (Japan: positive, r(176) = .57, p < .001; negative, r(176) = .24, p < .01; US: positive, r(194) = .41, p < .001; negative, r(194) = .41, p < .001 ).

The means and SDs of all scales in Study 2 are presented in Table 2. Because the difference in ARS between Japan and the US (computed in the same manner as in Study 1) was not significant, we did not control for ARS in Study 2.

Cross-Country Comparison

First, we conducted a one-way ANOVA to compare perceived relational mobility between Japan and the US. The analysis revealed a significant main effect of country, F(1, 372) = 52.05, p < .001, ηp² = .12, indicating that perceived relational mobility was again higher in the US than in Japan, consistent with Studies 1a and 1b. Next, we conducted a series of 2 (country: between-subjects) × 2 (valence: within-subjects) mixed-factor ANOVAs to examine whether perceptions and communication of positive and negative reputational information differed between countries. The distributions of scores for each condition are presented in Figure 3. For reputational perception, the results showed significant main effects of country and reputation valence. For the main effect of country, participants in the US reported a higher perceived prevalence of reputational information than participants in Japan, F(1, 372) = 85.17, p < .001, ηp² = .19. For reputation valence, participants reported greater perceived prevalence of positive than negative reputational information, F(1, 372) = 48.41, p < .001, ηp² = .12. The interaction between country and valence was also significant, F(1, 372) = 6.80, p = .009, ηp² = .02. As in Studies 1a and 1b, we then examined country differences separately for each valence using simple main effects analyses.

The p-values were adjusted using the Bonferroni method.

For positive reputational perception, the score was higher in the US than in Japan, mean difference = 0.777 (SE = 0.085), t(372) = 9.11, p < .001, d = 0.94, consistent with our prediction. For negative reputational perception, the score was also higher in the US than in Japan, mean difference = 0.393 (SE = 0.108), t(372) = 3.65, p <.001, d = 0.38, contrary to our prediction.

For reputational communication (i.e., participants' self-reported sharing), the results showed significant main effects of country and reputation valence. For the main effect of country, participants in the US reported greater overall communication of reputational information than participants in Japan, F(1, 372) = 101.96, p < .001, ηp² = .22. For reputation valence, participants reported greater communications of positive than negative reputational information, F(1, 372) = 371.98, p < .001, ηp² = .50. The interaction between country and valence was also significant, F(1, 372) = 18.76, p < .001, ηp² = .05. Simple main effects analyses revealed that, for positive reputational communication, the score was higher in the US than in Japan, mean difference = 0.949 (SE = .089), t(372) = 10.63, p < .001, d = 1.10, consistent with our prediction. For negative reputational communication, the score was also higher in the US than in Japan, mean difference = 0.331 (SE = .101), t(372) = 3.27, p < .01, d = 0.34, contrary to our prediction.

Figure 3. Distribution of reputational perception and communication in Japan and the US (Study 2).

Figure 3. Distribution of reputational perception and communication in Japan and the US (Study 2).

Indirect Effects via Relational Mobility

Next, we conducted mediation analyses to examine the indirect effects of country on reputational perceptions and communication via relational mobility. For positive reputation, the indirect effects were consistent with our prediction: higher perceived relational mobility in the US than in Japan was associated with both higher positive reputational perception and higher positive reputational communication. For negative reputation, the indirect effects were also consistent with our prediction: higher perceived relational mobility in the US than in Japan was associated with both lower negative reputational perception and lower negative reputational communication (Figure 4). It should be noted that the direct effects of country remained significant for both positive and negative reputational perception and communication, suggesting that factors other than perceived relational mobility may also contribute to these country differences. Note. All coefficients are standardised. *** p < .001, ** p < .01.

The main findings in Study 2 remained unchanged when participants excluded under criterion (f) were retained (see Supplementary Materials, Table S2). They also remained unchanged after controlling for age and gender (see Supplementary Materials, Table S4).

Discussion

Study 2 generally supported the predicted within-country associations between perceived relational mobility and the perceived prevalence and self-reported sharing of positive and negative reputational information. Higher perceived relational mobility was associated with a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing of positive reputational information, and with a lower perceived prevalence and less self-reported sharing of negative reputational information. However, in Japan, the associations with positive reputational sharing and negative reputational perception were not significant. The indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were consistent with our predictions for all four outcomes. In the between-country comparisons, participants in the US reported a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing of both positive and negative reputational information than those in Japan. The results for positive reputational information were consistent with our prediction, whereas those for negative reputational information were contrary to our prediction. We return to this unexpected pattern for negative reputational information in the General Discussion.

General Discussion

We examined how relational mobility, a socio-ecological factor pertaining to the degree of freedom of forming and selecting interpersonal relationships within a given social environment, is associated with the perceived prevalence and self-reported sharing of reputational information. Across three studies using US and Japanese adult samples, relational mobility was consistently higher in the US than in Japan. For positive reputation, the results generally supported our prediction. US participants reported a higher perceived prevalence (all studies) and more self-reported sharing (Study 2) of positive reputational information than Japanese participants, and the indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were consistent with our predictions in all studies. Within each country, higher perceived relational mobility was generally associated with a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing of positive reputational information, although these associations were not significant in the Japanese sample in Study 1b for perception and in Study 2 for sharing. For negative reputation, however, the results were mixed. Japanese participants did not report higher perceived prevalence or more selfreported sharing of negative reputational information than US participants; the country difference was either nonsignificant (Study 1b) or in the opposite direction (Studies 1a and 2). Nevertheless, the indirect effects via perceived relational mobility were consistent with our predictions in all studies. Within each country, lower perceived relational mobility was generally associated with a higher perceived prevalence and more self-reported sharing of negative reputational information, although the association with perception was not significant in the Japanese sample in Study 2.

These findings are broadly consistent with our theoretical account that positive and negative reputation sustain cooperation through distinct mechanisms. In low mobility contexts, where leaving existing relationships is difficult, negative reputation can deter norm violations because exclusion is particularly costly when alternative relationships are limited. In high relational mobility contexts, where individuals can readily form new relationships, positive reputation can provide an incentive for continued cooperation by increasing individuals' chances of being chosen as partners. Leaving the community, in contrast, means losing the benefits of an accumulated positive reputation, whereas the opportunity to leave reduces the deterrent power of negative reputation (Barclay, 2013; Hashimoto & Yamagishi, 2013; Wu et al., 2016; Yamagishi et al., 2008 Yamagishi et al., , 2009)). Although the present studies did not directly test these mechanisms, the indirect effects and within-country associations were generally consistent with this account. The country differences were also consistent with our predictions for positive, but not negative, reputational information. We discuss possible reasons for this discrepancy below.

These findings have several important theoretical implications. First, the findings suggest that both socio-ecological conditions and the valence of reputational information need to be considered when predicting its sharing and its consequences for cooperation. Previous research has suggested that socio-ecological conditions can shape reputation systems (Romano et al., 2021), but how these conditions relate to the sharing of positive versus negative reputational information has remained largely unexamined. Our findings suggest that relational mobility is associated differently with the sharing of positive and negative reputational information. To our knowledge, the present research is the first to extend the examination of these valence-specific associations beyond perceptions of others' sharing to individuals' self-reported sharing of reputational information.

Second, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of the socio-ecological bases of cross-cultural variation in psychological tendencies (Kitayama & Salvador, 2024). Recent research suggests that differences in reputation systems and expectations contribute to cross-cultural variation in psychological and behavioural tendencies, including avoidance of offending others (Hashimoto et al., 2011), types of interdependence (Uchida et al., 2019), emotional experiences of success (Maeda & Yuki, 2023) and the concealment of prosocial behaviour (Li et al., 2026). However, these studies have focused mainly on individuals' expectations about how others would evaluate them, leaving largely unexamined the informational environment from which such expectations may arise, that is, the reputational information that circulates in society. By assessing both perceived prevalence of others' sharing and individuals' self-reported sharing of positive and negative reputational information, the present research begins to address this gap. Future studies should further examine how reputational information circulates in different societies and how this circulation relates to cross-cultural variation in psychology.

Finally, the present findings suggest a possible link to the micro-macro dynamics through which social environments and individuals' psychological and behavioural tendencies mutually shape each other (cf. Baumard & André, 2025; Markus & Kitayama, 2010; Yamagishi & Hashimoto, 2016).

Relational mobility may influence which types of reputational information circulate, which in turn may shape individuals' reputational expectations and the behaviours that follow from them. In Study 2, individuals' self-reported sharing of reputational information was positively associated with their perceptions of others' sharing of information of the same valence. This association is consistent with the possibility that individuals not only respond to their reputational environment but also contribute to it through their own sharing. By examining both perceptions of others' sharing and individuals' self-reported sharing, the present research provides a starting point for investigating how reputational information environments and individual behaviour may shape each other.

Despite these contributions, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the within-country associations and indirect effects were generally consistent with our predictions, the country differences for negative reputational information were not. The perceived prevalence and selfreported sharing of negative reputational information were not higher in Japan than in the US; in Studies 1a and 2, they were higher in the US. This pattern suggests that factors other than perceived relational mobility may also contribute to these country differences. For example, norms about expressing negative evaluations may influence the perceived prevalence and sharing of negative reputational information. Future research across a wider range of societies should examine how relational mobility and other societal factors jointly relate to these outcomes.

Second, both perceived prevalence of others' sharing and participants' reports of their own sharing of reputational information relied on self-reports and may therefore have been susceptible to reporting biases. Participants may have had difficulty accurately recalling everyday reputational exchanges or may have been influenced by social desirability concerns, leading to over-or underreporting. Such concerns may be particularly strong when reporting one's own sharing of negative reputational information, because admitting to speaking ill of others may reflect poorly on oneself (Farley, 2011). In Study 2, self-reported sharing of negative reputational information yielded the lowest mean scores among the measures in both countries (Japan: M = 2.61; US: M = 2.94).

On the other hand, the low scores may reflect genuinely infrequent sharing rather than underreporting. Sharing such reputational information carries potential costs for the sender, such as the risks of incorrectly attributing misconduct to others (Anderson et al., 2020), retaliation (Balliet et al., 2020; Dores Cruz et al., 2021), or reputational damage to the sender (Farley, 2011). More broadly, negative expressions tend to be less frequent across languages (positivity bias; Dodds et al., 2015; Rozin et al., 2010), yet negative information can carry greater informational weight than positive information (Garcia et al., 2012; Rozin & Royzman, 2001). Moreover, it has been argued that the mere threat of

Within-Country Correlations

To test whether the predicted individual-level associations were observed within each country, we examined correlations between perceived relational mobility and reputational subscales separately in Japan and the US. For reputational perceptions, perceived relational mobility negatively correlated with negative reputational perception in the US, r(194) = -.20, p < .01, and showed a similar but nonsignificant trend in the same direction in Japan, r(176) = -.14, p = .06. Conversely, perceived relational mobility was positively correlated with positive reputational perception in both Japan, r(176) = .19, p < .01, and the US, r(194) = .34, p < .001.

For reputational communication, perceived relational mobility was negatively correlated with negative reputational communication in both Japan, r(176) = -.18, p < .05, and the US, r(194) = -.31, p < .001. Conversely, perceived relational mobility was positively correlated with positive reputational communication in the US, r(194) = .30, p < .001, but not in Japan, r(176) = .02, p = .84. Thus, although the country differences in negative reputational information were in the opposite direction to our prediction, the within-country associations were largely consistent with our predictions, with the exception of positive reputational communication in Japan.

negative reputation may suffice to deter defection, reducing the need to impose sanctions (Boyd & Richerson, 1992; Yamagishi & Suzuki, 2009). From this perspective, the frequency with which negative reputational information circulates may underestimate its functional importance, even in societies that rely heavily on it. The present data cannot distinguish between underreporting and genuinely infrequent sharing, and both may contribute to the low self-reported scores. Future research should employ behavioural methods to capture everyday reputational exchanges (cf. Dores Cruz et al., 2021).

Third, the associations of relational mobility with reputational perception and self-reported sharing were examined using correlational, cross-sectional data, which precludes causal inference.

Experiences of sharing reputational information or perceptions of its prevalence may, in turn, shape perceived or actual relational mobility, and unmeasured third variables may contribute to these associations. Additionally, because all measures relied on self-reports using the same six-point Likert response format within the same surveys, the observed associations may have been inflated by commonmethod variance (Podsakoff et al., 2003).

In addition, our theoretical account proposes that positive and negative reputational information play different roles in maintaining cooperation depending on relational mobility, and that people are more likely to share information that is more useful for this purpose. However, neither the proposed effects on cooperation nor the assumption about sharing was directly tested. Formal modelling and experimental approaches are therefore needed to examine these processes under varying levels of relational mobility.

In conclusion, the present studies represent an initial step towards understanding how positive and negative reputational information is shared in different societies. The findings suggest that relational mobility is associated differently with the perceived prevalence and self-reported sharing of positive and negative reputational information. Future research on reputation-based cooperation and relationship formation should consider both cross-societal variation in the sharing of reputational information and the functions that such information may serve.

The final analytic samples consisted of 281 participants in Study 1a (Japan: N = 140, 74 men, 65 women, 1 other; Mage = 41.61, SD = 10.75; US: N = 141, 72 men, 68 women, 1 other; Mage = 38.27, SD = 10.01) and 275 participants in Study 1b (Japan: N = 139, 78 men, 61 women; Mage = 42.35, SD = 11.48; US: N = 136, 74 men, 62 women; Mage = 39.58, SD = 12.33).
